extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic and philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply Mill's conceptual criteria for kinds of names, kinds of things (feelings, substances, attributes), and related distinctions (sensation vs object, perception, volition) as presented in a logic/metaphysics textbook chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative name
rubrics_metrics.description: A name is said to be relative when, over and above the object which it denotes, it implies in its signification the existence of another object, also deriving a denomination from the same fact which is the ground of the first name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variants: 'a name is relative when, being the name of one thing, its signification cannot be explained but by mentioning another' or 'when the name cannot be employed in discourse so as to have a meaning, unless the name of some other thing ... be either expressed or understood.' Example: 'father' and 'son' connote the same series of events but as attributes of different individuals. Implication: relative names carry connoted relations/actions grounded on facts involving two individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Univocal vs. æquivocal names
rubrics_metrics.description: A name is univocal when applied with respect to all things of which it can be predicated in the same sense; it is æquivocal when predicated of things in different senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'file' (steel instrument) vs 'file' (line of soldiers) are æquivocal — effectively different words that coincide in sound; ambiguous or equivocal use is treated as multiple distinct names rather than one. Implication: distinguish senses before reasoning to avoid fallacies arising from ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogical (metaphorical) use of names
rubrics_metrics.description: A name used analogically or metaphorically is predicated of two things not univocally but in significations somewhat similar, one being primary and the other a secondary, derived signification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'brilliant' applied to light (primary) and achievement (derived). Warning: common fallacious reasoning argues from a metaphorical expression as if literal; treat metaphorical predication as distinct in sense from the literal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition as object of logic
rubrics_metrics.description: A Proposition is discourse which affirms or denies something of some other thing; nothing but a Proposition can be an object of belief or of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: propositions consist of two names (subject and predicate) joined by a copula; to understand what can be affirmed or denied we must know what names signify. This grounds the need to enumerate kinds of things that can be predicates or subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of enumerating Existences (Categories) for Logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic requires an enumeration of all kinds of Things which are capable of being made predicates (the Categories or Predicaments were traditionally thought to be such an enumeration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill reviews and critiques the Aristotelian categories (Substance, Quantity, Quality, Relation, Action, Passion, Where, When, Position, Habit). He notes the list is redundant and defective, omits sensations and states of mind, and mixes distinct distinctions — indicating that a proper classification must be philosophically analyzed, not merely catalogued from ordinary language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful use of terms for 'existence' (being/entity/essence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete names corresponding to the abstract term 'Existence' (e.g., 'thing', 'being', 'entity', 'essence') are ambiguous and often biased toward substances rather than attributes or feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance to writers: select the term least likely to mislead in each case and be ready to employ imperfect words prudently; warning that rigorous adherence to a single sense may leave one without words to express certain ideas. Recognize that 'being' and 'substance' commonly connote self-existent things, while 'entity' and 'essence' have been transformed by usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feelings (states of consciousness) as a class of namable things
rubrics_metrics.description: Feelings, or states of consciousness, are a leading class of namable things; the term 'Feeling' is used in an enlarged sense to include Sensation, Emotion, Thought, and Volitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarification: 'thought' includes internal mental content (ideas, beliefs), distinguished from external objects of thought. Distinguish sensations from objects causing them and from attributes (e.g., sensation of white vs a white object vs whiteness). Sensations often lack one-word names and are commonly denoted by the object or attribute name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between sensation, object, and attribute
rubrics_metrics.description: A Sensation is to be carefully distinguished from the object which causes the sensation and from the attribute (quality) ascribed to the object in consequence of the sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: sensation of white vs white object vs whiteness. Sensations can be conceived independently of external causes (we can imagine sensations arising spontaneously). In practice language often conflates sensation and attribute; be aware of this to avoid conceptual confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between bodily states producing sensations and the sensations themselves; role of perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate the bodily state (physical processes in organs/brain) that precedes a sensation from the sensation (a state of mind); perception is sometimes posited as a separate act which recognizes an external object as cause of sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical point: sensations are states of mind; bodily states are not directly conscious. Some philosophers add 'perception' as an act (active recognition) rather than passive sensation; Mill treats perceptions as feelings (states of mind) and places detailed questions about their origin outside the scope of logic. Beware conflating psychological acts with external physical causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of feelings: Sensation, Thought, Emotion, Volition
rubrics_metrics.description: Feeling is a genus with subordinate species: Sensation, Emotion, and Thought; Mill adds Volitions as a fourth species among feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under 'thought' include all internal consciousness from imagery to abstract philosophical thought; 'emotion' covers affective states; 'volitions' are acts of will (intentions) which have special role for connotation of many names. Use these subdivisions when assigning a namable thing to the class of feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volitions (acts of the will) and action as volition + effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Volitions or acts of the will are active states of mind; an action consists of a volition (intention) followed by an effect — the volition and the consequent fact taken together constitute the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Importance: many relative names (e.g., sovereign/subject, physician/patient, mortgagor/mortgagee) connote large portions of actions (past, present, or possible future) and sometimes actions by others (legal consequences). When analyzing relational terms, account for the connoted volitions and their possible consequences. Example of action: intending to move the arm (volition) followed by the arm's movement (effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance vs Attribute (grammatical and philosophical distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: School logicians: an attribute must be the attribute 'of' something (e.g., color of something) and would cease if the something ceased; a substance is self-existent and need not be followed by 'of'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill criticizes the superficial grammatical account and notes problems (what is meant by 'of'?). He also notes metaphysical accounts that define substances as bodies or minds and that neither attributes nor substances can be cleanly imagined without reference to one another. Use a deeper philosophical analysis rather than mere grammatical criteria when classifying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body (substance) defined as external cause of sensations or as set of sensations joined by law
rubrics_metrics.description: A body, in modern metaphysical doctrine, may be defined as 'the external cause to which we ascribe our sensations.' Some idealist philosophers reduce body to the sensations themselves (or possibilities of sensation) combined according to a law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: recognize the philosophical controversy — whether belief in matter is intuitive or can be proved. Mill summarizes both positions: (1) bodies as external causes (substratum) producing ordered sets of sensations; (2) idealist view that objects are nothing but sensations and their laws. When analyzing 'substance', be explicit which account is being used and note epistemic limits: 'all we know of objects is the sensations which they give us and the order of the occurrence of those sensations.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemic limitation: all we know of objects is phenomenal
rubrics_metrics.description: All we know of objects is the sensations which they give us and the order of occurrence of those sensations; the real nature of the thing-in-itself (noumenon) remains unknowable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill cites Kant and others: even if one posits a universe of 'things in themselves', by our faculties we know only representations (phenomena). Implication for logic: classifications and talk of substances/attributes must acknowledge that our knowledge is of appearances (phenomena) rather than intrinsic natures.
